#### A call for redesigning American streets

![September 6, 2018: A call for redesigning American streets](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f66c44134aeaf736a7005e3c5)

**Duration:** 00:21:09

**Released:** 2018

**Series:** Better Off

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5tv31geSxNlyz9aGq1ivib)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

In this week’s podcast we’ll explore how America’s streets can be redesigned to benefit bicyclists and pedestrians—and we’ll explain why doing so may even help mitigate the effects of climate change. A new study from Anne Lusk, research scientist in the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzed how bicyclists and pedestrians responded to various placements of trees along cycle tracks—barrier-protected bicycle-exclusive paths between the road and the sidewalk. The research shows that the placement of these trees can play an important role in how people walking and biking perceive traffic, pollution, heat, and even safety. But the benefits extend beyond just those using the street—and could even be a factor in mitigating the effects of climate change. These trees may make it more likely that people will bike—helping to reduce pollution. And increased greenery can also help cool cities, which often suffer from a heat island effect, which means they’re significantly warmer than more rural areas. Lusk says all of this highlights the need to re-think how we’re designing streets to encourage more people to walk and bike instead of drive.

:::

About this episode:   Accumulating research has linked nitrogen dioxide emissions from gas stoves to exacerbated respiratory issues. A recent study from Case Western Reserve University set out to conduct a large analysis of whether switching to electric stoves could improve breathing conditions, but funding was halted just as early results came in showing significantly improved asthma symptoms. In this episode: what this truncated study can tell us about air quality inside our homes and what's lost when public health research is canceled. Guest:  Ana Rule, PhD, MHS, is an associate professor of Environmental Health and Engineering. Host:   Stephanie Desmon, MA, is a former journalist, author, and the director of public relations and communications for the Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs. #### How Congestion Pricing Can Impact Human Health

![How Congestion Pricing Can Impact Human Health](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fb592b5cfd7631d9aa38b898d)

**Duration:** 00:17:50

**Released:** 2024

**Series:** Science Friday

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/4SswOBTEVr46QtvHnhBriF)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/5UpA5Uw23B6bukC0TABffC)

In early June, New York Governor Kathy Hochul blocked a congestion pricing plan from going into effect in New York City. This plan would have charged a fee for cars to enter the central business district of Manhattan, and it would have been the first congestion pricing plan to be fully implemented in the United States.While congestion pricing can be costly for commuters, the fact that it keeps some cars off the road means it can have health benefits for surrounding communities. Successfully implemented congestion pricing plans in cities such as London, Singapore, and Stockholm have led to better air quality and health.SciFri’s John Dankosky sits down with Dr. Janet Currie, co-director of Princeton’s Center for Health and Wellbeing, and Dr. Andrea Titus, assistant professor of the Department of Population Health at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, to talk about the health impacts that congestion pricing has had around the world as well as the potential effects it could have in New York City and in other cities in the United States.Transcripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. The U.S. generates 292 million tons of trash each year – and that trash has to go somewhere.  Sometimes, that’s to an incinerator, where it’s burned and turned into electricity. Summer 2023 was a pretty scary one for the planet. Global temperatures in June and July reached record highs. And over in the North Atlantic Sea, the water temperature spiked to off-the-chart levels. Some people figured that meant we were about to go over the edge, doomsday. In the face of this, Hank Green (a long time environmentalist and science educator behind SciShow, Crash Course, and more), took to social media to put things in context, to keep people focused on what we can do about climate change. In the process, he came across a couple studies that suggested a reduction in sulfurous smog from cargo ships may have accidentally warmed the waters. And while Hank saw a silver lining around those smog clouds, the story he told—about smog clouds and cooling waters and the problem of geoengineering—took us on a rollercoaster ride of hope and terror. Ultimately, we had to wrestle with the question of what we should be doing about climate change, or what we should even talk about.Special thanks to Dr. Colin Carson and Avishay Artsy. Some things just go together: peanut butter and jelly, bacon and eggs, milk and cereal, London and smog. Or at least, that’s the way things used to be until the Great Smog of 1952. (Don’t worry, the first three pairings are safe). If you’ve watched The Crown, you may remember an early episode in which a thick, noxious smog surrounded the entire city of London for days on end. People coughing, hacking, collapsing. Traffic ground to a standstill. Authorities in denial. What was actually going on in December 1952 to lead to such conditions? What was in the smog to make it so toxic? And how did this severe pollution event lead to massive changes in air quality regulations around the world? Tune in to find out all this and more (including what The Crown got wrong). ##### This Is Canada's Worst Fire Season In Modern History. It's Not New

Canada is having its worst fire season in modern history. The fires have burnt more than 20 million acres, casting hazardous smoke over parts of the U.S. and stretching Canadian firefighting resources thin. Public officials and many news headlines have declared the fires as "unprecedented," and in the modern-sense they are. But NPR climate correspondent Nate Rott has been talking to researchers who focus on the history of wildfire in Canada's boreal forests and they say the situation is not without precedent.Want more stories on the environment? Two scenes. In the first, a doctor gets a call — the hospital she works at is having an outbreak of unknown origin, in the middle of the worst wildfire season on record. ##### Transcript

**0:00** · [ intro ] It seems like every workplace has that one person who swears that the potted spider plant sitting on their desk has an almost magical ability to purify the air in the office.

**0:14** · Are they actually onto something?

**0:15** · There is evidence to show that plants can remove pollutants from indoor air.

**0:19** · But a single potted plant probably won’t go the distance.

**0:22** · If you’ve heard that bringing plants into your home or office will improve your indoor air quality, you probably have a study conducted back in 1989 by NASA to thank for that meme.

**0:31** · The goal was to test whether a variety of types of indoor plants could be used for air purification, both on Earth and in space.

**0:38** · The plants were put into sealed containers, and the air pumped full of chemicals including benzene and formaldehyde.

**0:44** · Those chemicals fall under the broader umbrella of volatile organic compounds, or VOCs.

**0:50** · Some VOCs are known to cause health issues like headaches or liver and kidney damage.

**0:53** · And they’re noteworthy as indoor pollutants because household products and building materials can give them off.

**0:59** · The plants were kept under controlled conditions, with plenty of light and water and the air quality was measured over a 24 hour period.

**1:06** · The study found the majority of the plants included in the experiment removed much of the benzene and formaldehyde from the containers.

**1:11** · Plants are thought to remove pollutants from the surrounding air by absorbing the gases through their leaves and roots with some possible help from the microorganisms in the soil.

**1:19** · So that's it, right?

**1:20** · Houseplants help clean the air?

**1:21** · Well, not quite.

**1:22** · Later studies doing similar experiments have yielded mixed results.

**1:26** · A 2009 study tested 28 varieties of indoor plants and found four that were best at capturing every VOC the researchers threw at them.

**1:33** · So plants definitely can remove some pollutants in a laboratory test chamber.

**1:38** · But these idealized lab conditions don’t exactly represent the air in your office -- stuff like the amounts of light, water, and air circulation are all going to be different.

**1:47** · On top of that, the lab plants were purifying the air in a small area.

**1:52** · Some of the chambers in the NASA study were less than a cubic meter in volume.

**1:55** · That means for the same amount of purification to happen in your house, you would need an indoor rainforest.

**2:01** · One critic of the NASA study suggested that to get the same effect in a typical home you’d need about 680 separate plants.

**2:08** · There have been a handful of other studies investigating the effects of plants on indoor air quality, but at least one review, published in 2014, has attempted to take stock of the existing research.

**2:18** · And it concluded that, while lab-based studies generally show some effect, not many have been performed in living spaces, and the ones that have been done haven’t yielded a consensus.

**2:26** · So don’t count on your poor desk fern to fix all of your indoor air problems.

**2:31** · Thanks for watching this episode of SciShow, and thanks to Emma Hulton for asking.

**2:35** · To find out how to maybe get your questions answered, head over to patreon.com/scishow.

**2:39** · [ outro ]

###### lung and cardiac impact of smoke

**1:25** · But there are certain vulnerable populations that may have much more health impacts.

**1:31** · For example, someone who does have asthma, you know, is more at risk to have an asthma exacerbation when they breathe a smoke or someone with COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is that increased for a flare up when they inhaled the smoke?

**1:48** · there can be increases in heart attacks, arrhythmias.

**1:52** · There can be increases in stroke.

**1:54** · when the air quality gets bad, which can happen rapidly.

**1:57** · In the case of a fire, we see and feel the effects almost immediately.

**2:02** · there's there was a study showing that when it was a community in Canada, when they were exposed to the smoke within 2 hours there was increased in ambulance calls for respiratory distress and cardiac distress.

###### Maiya May talks about long-term trends

**2:22** · But I worry, will this trend continue forever?

**2:25** · Is it inevitable?

**2:26** · We asked Maiya May and our friends at Weathered to explain.

**2:30** · Is this part of a runaway train that we might call climate change?

**2:41** · Extreme wildfires basically need three things low humidity, high wind and an ignition source.

**2:48** · Climate change doesn't affect wind or ignition much, but it does make dry periods drier.

###### What is in wildfire smoke?

**4:25** · Well, obviously, it depends on what's burning, but combustion always produces pollutants.

**4:31** · One particularly harmful product is called particle pollution or particulate matter or PPM.

**4:38** · Scientists measure particle pollution by size.

**4:41** · For example.

**4:42** · PM10 particles are ten micrometers across PM 2.5 particles are 2.5 micrometers wide.

**4:50** · That's 40 times smaller than the smallest thing you can see with the naked eye.

**4:55** · By comparison, a human hair is 50 to 70 micrometers wide.

**4:59** · In the world of health and medicine.

**5:01** · You hear a lot about PM 2.5.

##### Transcript

**0:01** · The urban environment is a feat of human decision-making— from where to develop street grids lined with large glass office buildings, to which green spaces to preserve for outdoor recreation.

**0:13** · How humans make these choices, and the natural environment’s response, can create extremely different ecosystems in neighborhoods just a few blocks away from each other.

**0:23** · Researchers delved into dozens of studies to understand what drives these variations.

**0:29** · One well documented phenomenon in cities is the relationship between wealth and biodiversity.

**0:35** · More affluent areas generally have greater canopy cover, with larger, mature trees, as well as a higher diversity of birds.

**0:45** · This is known as the “luxury effect.”

**0:48** · Low-income areas typically have more man-made surfaces— including major heat-absorbers like asphalt and concrete, compared to higher-income areas.

**0:59** · The lack of shade from trees and vegetation, combined with more asphalt and concrete, makes it hotter in these neighborhoods— a phenomenon known as an “urban heat island.”

**1:10** · These communities are also more likely to be near sources of air pollutants, like expansive interstates pumping car exhaust.

**1:19** · Although wealth can sometimes predict the outcomes of an urban ecosystem, there isn’t always a clear relationship.

**1:26** · In some cases, the racial make-up of a neighborhood is better than income when forecasting canopy cover.

**1:33** · Researchers explored studies that highlight how systemic racism shaped our build environment.

**1:39** · One glaring example in the United States is residential segregation.

**1:44** · From 1933-1968, the federal government limited access to homeownership among Black Americans through a practice known as redlining.

**1:55** · Neighborhoods were graded based on the riskiness of providing a mortgage in the area.

**2:00** · The grades ranged from A, the most desirable areas, full of wealthy businessmen, to D, neighborhoods considered high-risk investments due to a combination of factors: from their environmental quality and distance from large industrial factories to the main determinant, the presence of foreign-born and Black people.

**2:22** · The inability for Black people to buy homes in these neighborhoods meant many types of capital investments left— landlords abandoned their properties, and public services, such as transportation and park maintenance, weren’t prioritized.

**2:36** · Today, many U.S. cities still exhibit long-lasting environmental impacts from this discrimination.

**2:42** · Neighborhoods which had a “D” grade in the 60s have about half the canopy cover of historically white communities.

**2:50** · Some studies evaluate how the current environment relates to historically redlined communities, but researchers did not find any research that traces how ecosystems changed over time because of this segregation.

**3:03** · They propose that because habitable regions are more spread out in these areas, animal populations struggle to breed since they are cut off from each other.

**3:14** · The reduced breeding options for animals could have decreased gene diversity, an important way for animals to adapt to changing environments.

**3:23** · And decreased gene flow of native species could promote the abundance of pest species, like mosquitos and brown rats, which carry diseases that can infect humans.

**3:34** · The combination of all these outcomes— from urban heat islands to increased pests— make low-income, marginalized communities far more vulnerable to risks like climate change.

**3:47** · Scientists say such evidence shows that conservation and social justice cross paths— especially along neighborhood streets.

##### Transcript

**0:01** · If you imagine a typical American city street, and you take away the space that’s dedicated to cars, you aren’t left with very much.

**0:09** · There are some narrow walkways on the side, and some bridges in between them, but not much else.

**0:13** · Cars dominate cities.

**0:16** · Spend some time walking around most cities and you’ll find yourself pushed to narrow sidewalks, waiting for crosswalk lights.

**0:20** · You’ll find cyclists navigating really narrow strips of space.

**0:23** · Americans are used to cars the way that fish are used to water.

**0:28** · That’s so ubiquitous in the U.S. that I think for most people, it just never occurred to them that it could be otherwise.

**0:35** · But what if there were a way to change that?

**0:36** · To give space back to pedestrians and bicyclists, and to make cities more friendly to life outside of a car?

**0:43** · It turns out Barcelona might have a solution.

**0:48** · In 2014, the city was faced with serious air pollution problems.

**0:51** · Barcelona and its 35 surrounding municipalities consistently failed to meet the EU’s air quality targets.

**0:57** · Studies were showing that air pollution in the region causes 3,500 premature deaths every year.

**1:03** · Traffic in the city also causes severe noise pollution.

**1:05** · So the city developed an extensive Urban Mobility Plan with the hope of reducing traffic by 21 percent.

**1:11** · The coolest part of the plan were these things: They call them "superilles".

**1:17** · Superilles?

**1:18** · “Si, superilles.”

**1:19** · That translates to “superblocks”.

**1:21** · It’s this urban design concept intended to minimize the presence of cars in city centers.

**1:26** · The word “superblock” has been used before to describe huge city blocks without any passageways for cars.

**1:31** · But that’s not what’s happening here.

**1:33** · So here’s how Barcelona’s plan works.

**1:35** · You take nine square city blocks and close off the inside to through traffic.

**1:39** · So buses, big freight trucks — or any vehicles that are trying to get from one part of town to the next — have to drive around the perimeter.

**1:47** · Inside the superblock, the speed limit is kept to 10 kilometers per hour — that translates to just over 6 miles per hour — and curbside parking is replaced by underground parking.

**1:55** · That means you wind up with street space for markets, outdoor games, and events.

**2:00** · Within this nine square block perimeter you're gonna have kind of a pleasant streetscape where people can walk around and mingle and do things without this kind of constant fear of cars around.

**2:13** · The concept is going to be tested out in five neighborhoods, but the city has identified 120 possible intersections throughout the region where it could be implemented.

**2:22** · So how do we know what the results of this kind of plan would look like?

**2:24** · Well, northwest of Barcelona is a city called Vitoria-Gasteiz, which has implemented superblock designs since 2008.

**2:30** · In the main superblock at the city center, pedestrian space increased from 45 percent of the total surface area to 74 percent.

**2:37** · With so much less traffic, noise levels dropped from 66.5 dBA to 61 dBA.

**0:01** · [Narrator] Wildfire smoke is loaded with harmful particles like charred plant matter, incinerated materials, and noxious gases. But it's also carrying stuff that's alive, thousands of teeny-tiny microorganisms like bacteria and fungi.

**0:15** · But why doesn't the heat from a wildfire kill all these microorganisms?

**0:19** · Well, not all parts of a wildfire are hot.

**0:23** · When we look at fire on the scale of a microorganism, there are likely pockets of cold air, areas that are not being burned at all.

**0:32** · [Narrator] In those tiny pockets of cooler air, microorganisms can catch rides on bits of carbon, or water vapor, rise high into the atmosphere and travel long distances. And some could potentially infect humans. Some health experts are already noticing a concerning relationship between wildfire smoke exposure and rates of infection. One study in California found an uptick in fungal infections after wildfires within a 200-mile radius of hospitals. And climate change is making wildfires more intense and more impactful.

**1:08** · Compared to the yearly average in the 1970s, the average wildfire season in the US is now 105 days longer, burns six times the number of acres and has three times as many large fires.

**1:21** · Fires are affected by dry conditions and warmer conditions. Climate change is causing more of those extremes. More extreme conditions, more extreme wildfires. They go together, hand by hand.

**1:34** · [Narrator] Though there are still many unknowns, risk is growing for more people.

###### Intro

**0:00** · Search Google Earth for China and you’ll see this.

**0:03** · But an unedited satellite photo might look more like this.

**0:08** · That gray smudge is air pollution and it’s coming from Chinese cars, factories, and power plants.

**0:13** · But it’s not only here.

**0:14** · In cities around the world, air pollution is a big problem.

**0:18** · A majority of humans now live in cities and that number is only going to rise, which means more cars, more factories, and more power plants.

**0:25** · As officials explore options for fighting air pollution, there is one tool that is often overlooked: trees.

###### Air pollution

**0:35** · Cities are centers of industry, but the resulting pollution is filling our lungs and making us sick.

**0:41** · One major culprit is particulate matter: airborne particles of dust, soot and smoke that are released when we burn fossil fuels or kicked up during construction and farming.

**0:49** · When we inhale them, they can cause asthma and they can also enter our bloodstream to cause strokes and even death.

**0:54** · Experts estimate that outdoor air pollution kills over three million people a year and as cities grow, leaders are funding creative—and often expensive—solutions for the problem.

**1:04** · In London, the mayor spent over a million pounds spraying city streets with an adhesive that was supposed to glue pollutants to the road.

**1:10** · and in the Netherlands, designers have created a giant air purifier they call "The Smog Free Tower", which is cool, but there is another, simpler solution… A new report from The Nature Conservancy shows that planting trees can be a cost-effective way to improve public health, which they do in two ways: First, a tree removes particulate matter when polluted air blows through its branches.

###### Planting trees

**1:31** · The particulate matter settles on the leaves and when it rains the dust is washed down the gutter so we don’t inhale it.

**1:37** · Second, trees cool temperatures by providing shade and releasing water through photosynthesis, which cools summer temperatures by about two to four degrees fahrenheit.

**1:46** · But there is a catch!

**1:47** · Trees can only clean and cool the air within a close radius: about one hundred feet, so city officials need to be careful where they plant.

**1:54** · Officials can maximize pollution reduction by planting trees where population density and air pollution overlap.

**1:59** · The Nature Conservancy report uses data from Washington D.C. to create a map showing where planting trees will have the highest return on investment.

**2:06** · And some trees work better than others: trees with larger, stickier leaves, like maples and elms are more effective, but they also need to be considered within the larger ecosystem.

**2:15** · Compared to DC, many cities around the world have even more to gain from planting trees: this map shows where return on investment is highest for reducing particulate matter.

**2:23** · With proper targeting, planting trees can be just as cost-effective as other strategies like converting public transportation to use less diesel fuel.

**2:30** · But there is one major limiting factor: water access.

**2:34** · What might work in Boston, will be less feasible in a city like Doha, Qatar, where water is a scarce resource.

**2:39** · And on top of that, many mayors don’t yet think of trees as a public health resource.

**2:44** · Trees might not look like giant air filters, but that’s exactly what they are, and the sooner we start thinking of them that way, the sooner the air we breathe might be cooler and cleaner in cities around the world.

###### Why we need better waste management

**1:31** · Zoë Lenkiewicz is one of the founding members of Wasteaid, and has been a waste manager for over 20 years.

**1:38** · “It also generates dioxins and furans, which are known to cause cancer.

**1:41** · All of this is going into the local air, wherever people are burning waste.”

**1:48** · Women are more directly impacted, as they are often responsible for disposing of household waste.

**1:53** · Burning trash this way is a serious problem. But done differently, there are advantages to it.

###### Waste to energy

**2:01** · Here’s where controlled burning, aka incineration, comes in.

**2:04** · Incinerators first appeared where it was hard to landfill, in London in 1874, then in New York City, in 1885.

**2:12** · “The incineration process itself, it reduces the volume of the waste [by] 90 percent.”

**2:19** · Ella Stengler is the managing director of the umbrella organization for European waste to energy operators.

**2:25** · “And it fulfills the kind of sanitary task because it destroys the pollutants which are embedded in the waste.”

**2:32** · The generated heat can also be turned into energy. It's called, unsurprisingly, waste to energy.

**2:38** · In the US, where there’s a lot of space and cheap energy in the form of oil, waste to energy wasn’t so competitive, and many plants were closed.

**2:46** · But more and more plants were built in the EU.

**2:50** · Today they provide power to 18 million Europeans, and heat to 15 million.

**2:56** · They’re a common waste management option for countries like Denmark and the Netherlands, which have almost completely eliminated landfilling.

**3:05** · Environmental organizations see potential in waste to energy as a transition step toward a more circular economy, especially in countries without much space, that need more energy.

**3:18** · Here’s how the plants work: The garbage is dumped into a big pit — from there it’s fed into the furnaces.

**3:25** · They burn extremely hot, and the waste is reduced in a matter of minutes.

**3:30** · The heat from the fires generates steam, which turns turbines to create electricity.

**3:35** · The steam can also be used for heating.

**3:38** · The 10% that doesn’t burn is called bottom ash, and metals can be recovered from it.

**3:44** · The rest can then be used as construction material.

**3:50** · So the process reduces the volume of waste, creates energy, and part of the residue can even be recycled.

**3:58** · What’s not to love?

**4:01** · Well, there are a few reasons why the world isn’t full of waste to energy plants with ski slopes on top.

**4:07** · One of those reasons is fly ash, which is everything caught by the filters.

**4:11** · It needs to be disposed of in a hazardous waste facility.

**4:15** · Another reason is cost.

**4:16** · “If there would be a waste to energy plant built, it should be equipped with a state-of-the-art technology, which is expensive.

**4:27** · And you need to train the staff to properly operate it and also authorities to monitor it.”

**4:33** · Even without ski slopes, waste to energy plants can cost over one billion US dollars to build.

**4:39** · Without the latest technology and monitoring, pollution can reach unsafe levels, and impact people living nearby.

**4:47** · And they also emit a lot of CO2: in the EU, around 52 million tonnes per year.

**4:56** · That’s like 430,000 cars each driving a million kilometers.

**5:02** · “Policymakers and industries put incineration in the same type of energy group as renewables, like wind or solar or even nuclear."

**5:15** · This is Tatiana Lujan.

**5:16** · She leads the plastics team for ClientEarth, and is also working to implement the EU's circular economy directive.

**5:24** · “But when you look at the greenhouse gas emissions of incineration, they're actually pretty close to coal and gas, and way far from wind, solar, nuclear.

**5:36** · A study commissioned by ClientEarth found that controlled incineration generates between 59 and 73% of the emissions that coal would.

**5:44** · Classifying this energy as renewable can divert funding from more sustainable waste management technologies like recycling.

**5:51** · So, where it can be correctly built and managed, controlled incineration is better than a landfill – but it’s by far not the cleanest option to handle waste, no matter how much energy is won.

###### The Waste Hierarchy

**6:04** · Have a look at this “waste hierarchy pyramid” – bear with me, it’s less complicated than it looks.

**6:09** · At the very bottom of the pyramid is open burning or dumping, the worst possible way to get rid of trash.

**6:15** · Disposal without energy recovery is next, so landfilling or incineration without energy generation.

**6:22** · Then here’s where waste to energy, which is an umbrella term for a few different methods, comes in.

**6:29** · Then comes recycling.

**6:31** · Even better is to re-use things, often called upcycling, and at the top is prevention and reduction.

**6:38** · Yeah, the whole world is pretty far from the top.

**6:42** · That is why waste to energy is seen by some as a quick “solution” for countries struggling with their waste.

###### A waste solution for the Global South?

**6:51** · Not surprisingly, plants are opening up around the world, like in China, Indonesia and India.

**7:02** · Africa’s first waste to energy plant just opened, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

**7:08** · But it has proven to be more complicated than just opening up plants and burning the problem away.

**7:14** · One reason is that the composition of waste varies widely throughout the world.

**7:22** · “You can't take one model that works in a wealthy country like a cookie cutter and expect it to work in a low-income country because it's a completely different market.”

**7:34** · In India, household waste is around 50 percent organic matter, like food scraps, which are too wet to burn.

**7:41** · And because of the lack of centralized waste collection, trash there is often mixed together.

**7:48** · “I don't think segregation is happening at all in majority of the Indian cities.

**7:55** · So that's a major, major problem.”

**7:57** · Pritpal Randhawa has been conducting long-term studies on waste management in India for the past 10 years.

**8:02** · “The waste has to be segregated and the undesirable material should be separated from that waste, and only the waste with high calorific value should be burned.

**8:14** · But that is not something which is happening actually.”

**8:18** · Calorific value is a measure of a substance’s heating power — in other words, how easily it burns.

**8:24** · Crude oil and mixed plastics come in at around 40 megajoules per kilogram.

**8:29** · Food is about 16.

**8:31** · Without waste separation, lots of food scraps find their way to the furnaces, forcing the plants to add additional fuel.

**8:39** · This makes the whole facility extremely inefficient.

**8:42** · Countries also need to have a place to store the hazardous waste.

**8:46** · So if incineration isn’t a silver bullet for the Global South, what are other options?

**8:52** · “It’s not very complicated at all – the ideal situation would be management of waste at the decentralized level.”

**9:01** · And not only decentral, but diversified: specifically suited to the environment and economy of an area.

**9:10** · In many cities in India, for example, waste pickers collect recyclables, which are processed informally.

**9:15** · Biogas generated from organic waste can be a source of fuel from Benin to Mumbai.

**9:20** · And plastic can be made into building material.

**9:25** · “With waste management, absolutely one size does not fit all.

**9:28** · And you really need to look at what's most appropriate for that local area.”

###### When incineration makes sense

**9:34** · Waste to energy plants can work, but a trash collection system and a strong environmental regulator are both necessary.

**9:41** · These can be really hard to come by.

**9:44** · Even with them, countries need to do some careful reflection before building new plants.

**9:48** · “When you create incineration, you're making huge investments and locking yourself in a system that you're going to have to continue feeding and feeding and feeding.

**10:00** · And that creates a disincentive for transitioning to a real circular economy.”

**10:08** · So before more trash burning facilities join the global system, policymakers should look at funding more sustainable methods of waste disposal – like recycling, reusing and most importantly, reducing our waste in the first place.

**10:22** · So what do you think?

**10:24** · To burn, or not to burn?

**10:28** · If this video made you think at all...

##### Description

If cars are bad for the climate, and public transport good, what makes people switch? From Jakarta to Tallinn, cities are trying to motivate people by eliminating fares. Let’s check if that works.



We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.
